September 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 3
As the Guild begins its next quarter century, we are
in full swing returning to visiting demonstrators
with demos and classes. By press time Tom Wirsing
has come and gone and presented us with an excellent demonstration on turning a platter with his innovative and measured approach and he offered
some very keen insight into various tool steels and
using the correct sharpening abrade to get them
sharp. If you missed the demo I recommend watching it on our private Youtube when it becomes
available.
Being our Twenty-Fifth Anniversary we are marking the milestone over the next two months. Mike
Hosaluk is here for September as our feature demonstrator and he will present the only activity
during that night! For anyone that has been turning
for more than ten years Mike needs little introduction. He is one of the world’s outstanding turners
and instructors and has inspired and taught thousands of turners worldwide. During the October
meeting we will have a potpourri of things happening to help mark the 25th!
Next spring we have Mark Gardner visiting with a
demo and a class. Very possibly Melissa Engler and
Graeme Priddle will be able to pay us a visit too. I
am working to confirm them in the next few weeks.
If you have already registered online you’ll note
that we have integrated a payment option for your
convenience. Thank you to Bill Fowle for making
this happen.
Steve
President’s Challenge:

October - End grain bowl with carved feet
Welcome to a new turning season! Hope you all
had a great summer.
Brian Lunt has, I believe, set a new newsletter record for the most articles in a single newsletter (at
least since I’ve been editor/publisher) with 4 very
engaging articles you should all find interesting.
This month’s Member Profile features long-time
member, Ross Pilgrim. Our safety article this
month is a caution about CA glue by Brian Andrews.
I hope you enjoy this month’s newsletter and hope
that this month’s collection of articles by The Two
Brians will inspire more members to take keyboard
in hand and create so great new content for our
little publication.
Steve

September 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
I was asked to make some
display stands for a non
profit organization raising
funds to save the Speckled
Bear in the Machu Picchu
area of Peru and employ local women.
The first two displays have gone to the Museum Of
Anthropology at UBC and VGH gift shop. 10 are in
transit to other locations.
These displays show Feltis Christmas Tree Ornaments made of sheep’s wool and are made by indigenous people in Peru.
https://sbc-peru.org/what-we-do/communityempowerment/
I used my lathe in several different ways to create
these displays.
Dollarama was a great economical source for this
project.
You start with packs of 3/8” wooden dowels and
cut them to the right length on the bandsaw.
Then you use a collet chuck to turn a “Button
Bead” on one end. You make lots of these. You can
use detail gouges or a carbide round tool. Lots of
options.
Then put a 1” dowel between lathe centres and
make all your marks from a story stick.
(Continued on page 5)

September 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
While mounted on the lathe, create a ¾” dia. tenon
to fit in the main base and round off the other end.
Later we band sawed a kerf slot to hold a laminated placard.
Drill all the marked holes using a jig on the drill
press.
Cut 10” diameter disks from birch or maple plywood and drill a 3/4” centre hole. Then make
round “donuts” to add support for the centre post.
I airbrushed the stain and Emtech water based lacquer on all the wood parts.
Used a tapered wood dowel as a holder for staining
the base
To remain cost effective, we bought clear “Lazy Susan’s” from Dollarama and, dissembled them,
which was easy, then mounted them with a pin jaw
and moved a live centre with a cone up to increase
stability against the interior. Then cut the cylinder
part away to end up with just the flat (and cheap)
rotational base.
Used a gouge to clear off any sharp edges and
touched up with sandpaper.
Trimmed the centre post to fit flush with the base
and mounted the turntable to the base. This also
makes a simple painting/ spraying platter for your
shop.
The reaction has been very positive so I expect I
will be making lots more of these.
(Continued from page 4)

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild

Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
I was born in Nanaimo BC, and have lived in the
Vancouver area most of his life, currently residing
in North Vancouver. I am a retired Chartered Accountant who spent his business career as a financial manager and executive with a large BC corporation.
I started woodturning in 1998 after enjoying this
portion of high school woodworking classes. My
skills have improved through observing demonstrations and taking courses offered locally by world
class turners. I am inspired by the natural beauty of
wood and my work emphasizes the natural colour
and grain of the selected woods. I also attempt to
retain function of the piece as well as artistic qualities.
Most of the wood I use is from unwanted trees
that have been removed due to death, disease or
construction and would otherwise be burned as
firewood or taken to the landfill.
There are many beautiful woods not native to
British Columbia. Unfortunately they are only available in standard boards rather than turning blocks.
Segmented turning allows small quantities of these
harvested exotic hardwoods to be used for colour
in my segmented work.
My turnings have been recognized locally, West
Coast Woodturning Competition as well as Wood
Coop Gallery, and internationally have been included in the following publications:
•
500 Wood Bowls: Bold and Original Designs
Blending Tradition & Innovation, Lark Books,
Katherine Duncan-Aimone, Ray Leier, and Jan
Peters, 2004
•
Woodturning Magazine: Letter from America,
GMC Publications, Vol. 109 2002.
•
American Woodturner: Pasadena Instant Gallery, Journal of the American Association of
Woodturners, Vol. 18.3 Fall 2003.
•
Woodturning Magazine: Letter from America,
GMC Publications, Vol. 146 2005.
I am an active member of The American Associa-
(Continued on page 7)

tion of Woodturners and The Greater Vancouver
Woodturners Guild where I have demonstrated
turning fundamentals and constructing segmented
bowls.
Always liked working with wood. Through teen
years family built 3 houses and cousins and I
worked on most of the forming, framing, sheeting
and roofing.
Enjoyed Woodwork Shop course throughout High
School, Lathes were available but training very
basic.
Was the general contractor on our own home, did
much of the finishing woodwork, and made sure it
had a wood shop where I built skills with a router
making Crib Boards and finger joint boxes .
When a relative passed he left an 8”x24” Rockwell
Beaver lathe which ended in my shop and sat for
10 years gathering dust.
When I retired the first time at 55, I got in the way
too much and my wife finally told me to go down
and learn to use uncle Al’s lathe!
I was an acquaintance of Sandy Dougal, one of the
early members of the GVWG that was just starting
up. He gave me some basic training and more importantly invited me to the “new Guild” starting in
Coquitlam
I joined the Guild and met members that were in
early stages of learning as well as members and
local and international demonstrators that were
accomplished at the craft. Most of the demonstrators also taught 1 – 3 day hands on courses using
KMS Classroom.
In early years I regularly attended the annual
woodturning Symposium in Provo Utah, which was
probably the most important step in deciding “this
is my life-long hobby”
Tell us about your workshop/studio.
•
300 square feet in the basement, next to furnace, with window and decent lighting
•
Table saw, Chop saw, Band saw, Scroll saw, Disc
sander, thickness planer Drill press
•
Oneway, 24x36 Lathe with outboard bed extension
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
•
3/8 & ½” bowl gouges
•
3/8 & ½” spindle gouges
•
18” exchangeable soft grip handles
•
1” roughing gouge
What is your favourite wood?
•
For the first 10 years I was mainly doing segmented turning which used very colourful imported
hardwoods
often
with
unique/
pronounced grains. Most of my turnings for the
Wood Coop Gallery were segmented.
•
With that Gallery Shrinking in size in 2010 and
the availability of exotic hardwoods significantly diminishing I have reduced my segmented
turnings and gone to local “hardwoods” mainly
Western Big Leaf Maple.

WBLM Burl is my preference for saleable pieces.
•
WBLM is my preference for bowls, but I also
use other local hardwoods as the become available, especially if they have colour or feathery
grain
What finishes do you prefer using?
•
Segmented - only Tung Oil
•
Non-segmented current pieces tend to be
functional so usually use walnut oil as base preservative with Clapham’s Beeswax or Mahoney’s OilWax as the top coat
Do you ever incorporate other materials into
your pieces?
•
Lots of CA Glue …. (haha)
•
Segmented sections in otherwise solid pieces
What other types of woodworking or pursuits
do you have?
Still occasionally make things using router.
What inspires you – where do you get your
ideas from?
•
I don’t have a lot of ideas so most of my solid
pieces have common shapes that I have enhanced with various ways of burning, burnishing, placement of natural grain, use of burl sections etc.
•
My wife is an accomplished Quilter and quilt
patterns provided ideas for my segmented
work
Who has been the greatest influence on your
work?
•
Curt Theobald’s work got my mind into segmented turning. He has always been available
to me to bounce ideas off and provide direction.
•
The guild bringing in multiple world class turners in the early days was an excellent starting
point.

work?

Unlike most other glues, CA Glue comes with a few
noticeable health warnings and cautions. As wood
turners, we need to know and heed these warnings
and take the appropriate steps to avoid the health
hazards associated to the use of CA glue.
A brief search for Safety Data Sheets associated
with Cyanoacrylate will demonstrate that the following health issues are present:
•
Combustible liquid
•
Causes skin irritation.
•
Causes serious eye irritation.
•
Suspected of causing cancer.
•
May cause respiratory irritation.
It should ne noted that the effects of exposure to
CA Glue is accumulative. That is over time the
effects of exposure to CA glue will build.
Extreme Caution must be exercised when using
heat with CA Glue. At certain higher temperatures
CA Glue will vaporize forming deadly cyanide gas.
CA Glue is a mainstay in the world of crime scene
examinations. The CA Glue is lightly heated in a
controlled manner with higher humidity and the
fumes
will
visualize
friction
ridge
detail
(fingerprints) on non-porous surfaces HOWEVER it
is always used within a specific chamber that is
well ventilated and results in no exposure to the
user.

Many A/V volunteers have made our guild
meetings run well in the past. Lots of them are still
current guild members.
Each group kept our guild on top of new technologies available at the time and thanks to them we
have the strong foundation that we stand on today.
On a hot summer August day, our current AV Team
got together to rebuild our manuals and set the
standards required for our more complicated system. This has been a technological challenge since
Covid to have the option of live, Zoom and recorded meetings for all to enjoy.
Thank you to Shawn Preus, Matt Lo and Bob Gilson
for your dedication and expertise and keeping me
sane during this process.
We are always looking for assistance. If you would
like to help out, we need extra hands pulling gear
out of the storage room, laying out cables, setting
up camera stands then putting it all away after the
meeting.
Ask any of us and we can show you what we need
to set up in time and take down for a successful
guild night or Saturday Demo.
A typical guild night setup
GVWG A/V Team

Shopping at KMS Tools means you can help your
club earn credit - approximately 2% on your purchase. For instance, we recently used some of our
credit to buy the brand-new Laguna demo lathe
that we use for Focus on Fundamentals! All you
need to do is to link your name/phone number to
the GVWG and you’re done. The easiest way to do
this is to go online to: https://www.kmstools.com/
group-rewards and fill in a short form. In doing so,
you also become a KMS Club member and benefit
from better pricing on their full line of products. As
a friendly reminder if you are already a KMS Club
member, it is worthwhile to check that you are also
linked to the GVWG for us to receive the credits.

Here’s an idea to do when you have lots of excess
paper around (like we did after rewriting our guild
AV Manual). And it’s another excuse to use old
wood glue.
Cut the 8 1-2” x 11” paper in 4 squares (same size
as our guild gallery tags) and stack in a pile. I use a
shop square to line up the edges.
Put a spare paper on top and bottom to give you a
barrier after the glue is cured. Ask me how I found
this out decades ago! Place a heavy weight on top
to compress the stack. I used my large chuck and
jaws.
Apply any wood glue you have in your shop with a
paint brush to one end of this stack. The first coat
is important to get into each line of paper so when
you are done they are all stuck together. I use a
few coats of glue.
Slice them up in packs with an Exacto knife and
make your first note !

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 34)

September 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 34
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
